entries.summary: Now that code ships faster than ever, you have more time to spend on projects just for the fun of it. Here's what we can learn through that process as developers.
entries.text: As kids, we spent hours tinkering and building and just messing with things. As an adult, I could watch my own young kiddos figure out how certain shapes and movement work all day. Through that play, we improved our problem-solving and language skills, and it’s probably not a stretch to say it was good for our early engineering skills. In this era of development now, we’re starting to get a taste of that again. We’re experimenting more, and taking in more changes, because it’s all new! For the last four years at GitHub Universe, we’ve had hackable conference badges. What started as a simple e-ink display for your name and job title morphed into a labor of love for Martin Woodward, VP of Developer Relations. This year, the badge evolved into a device with a color screen, rechargeable battery, accelerometer sensors, and touch-sensitive gaming controls. The tinkering we’ve seen with the badges has been amazing. entries.summary: Learn how to assess a legacy application, choose a bounded modernization step, and reuse the method with a GitHub Copilot agent skill.
entries.text: A request to modernize an application often starts with a technology question: Which framework should replace the old one? Before you choose, find out what still works. Then collect evidence that can act as a regression net for that behavior and show where modernization is necessary. I used an evidence-first method on four public applications, from a small Node.js game to a large Java enterprise resource planning (ERP) application. Each needed a different treatment, but the way I collected evidence, chose the next experiment, and decided on possible proof points was repeatable. This post walks through that process so you can apply it to one application of your own. It also shows how to encode the procedure in a GitHub Copilot agent skill while keeping architectural judgment with the people responsible for the system. Build evidence before choosing a target The label on an application rarely tells you enough. “Java microservices” doesn’t tell you which Java Development Kit (JDK) runs in production, where that version is pinned, whether the tests execute, or which interfaces other systems depend on. “Legacy monolith” doesn’t tell you whether the business core is broken or whether one retired platform dependency prevents the application from starting. entries.title: How to choose the next safe step in application modernization

entries.summary: Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion.
entries.text: In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities. Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine. Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework. I attended John Maeda’s session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed. entries.summary: In the Codename MDASH pilot, GitHub and Microsoft turned thousands of raw AI findings into 99 checked, private reports with suggested fixes for six widely used open source projects.
entries.text: AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings. Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports. As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it. AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings? GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH, Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on. The process Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked: Find. Codename MDASH, an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found. Filter. entries.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.

entries.summary: Discover how we built the open Agent Host Protocol to keep your agent sessions accessible across editors, apps, phones, and the cloud.
entries.text: Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices. In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows. Why one integration per client stopped working GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have. At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. entries.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices

entries.summary: In October, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services. The post GitHub availability report: October 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.text: We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability. The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery. As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity. That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range. We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. entries.summary: Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.
entries.text: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database. I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”. Define one job and when it applies A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose: name: proof-agen
entries.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills

entries.summary: Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports.
entries.text: Editor’s note (November 17, 2026): This post has been updated with additional CVE information and updated guidance for GitHub Enterprise Server users. Please see the release information below for the versions that include the fixes. Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution when cloning malicious repositories Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker-controlled Git server can exploit this discrepancy to replace a clone’s .git file or directory, redirecting Git to attacker-controlled configuration or hooks. For recursive clones, this can execute attacker-controlled code during the clone. For non-recursive clones, an attacker can replace the top-level .git directory with a file pointing to attacker-control

entries.summary: Writing code got faster. The work around it didn't. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.
entries.text: This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year? Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption. As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub. Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working.
